As hypothesized, the Snail Kites in the Palo Verde National Park marsh were shown to be highly selective for snail size, as is illustrated by Figure 1, with mean operculum size in perches significantly higher than mean operculum size for transects. These findings are

concurrent with past studies and with the general biology of the Snail Kite itself. Because the Snail Kite hunts by sight, it is conceivable that it can locate a larger snail more easily. Also, a larger snail has a larger opening to the operculum, which is more easily removed by using the Kite's long, curved bill.⁴ Furthermore, the Snail Kite captures its prey using its talons, so a larger snail is more easily grasped by the talons of the Kite. This further promotes the theory that by selecting for larger prey, the Kite is most efficient in energy usage. The Kite receives a greater caloric intake to compensate for energy expended in the capturing process by selecting for larger snails.¹ One study notes that a breeding Snail Kite couple will select increasingly larger snails as the distance from the nest increases, again showing the most efficient use of energy.¹ The significantly lower mean size of the snails in the live population of this study suggests that larger snails are more rare in the habitat, which can be problematic for the Kite who is selective for these larger size snails. However, Janzen and Reed (1999) suggest that larger snails spend more time near the surface and are therefore more easily captured. Our study indicates that while it may be true that larger snails spend more time on the surface, they are more rare within the snail population and therefore less easily captured. It would be useful to take measurements of surface durations for different size snails to more clearly address whether larger snails actually spend more time at the surface. Also, a study with a larger sampling pool could reveal greater certainty as to whether larger snails are in fact more rare in the population.

Although Snail Kites were selective for snail size in this study, they had no preference for snail shell color, with nearly equal amounts of light and dark shells found in both transects and perches. Because Snail Kites hunt by site, it was expected that a lighter color shell would be more visible to the Kite and therefore captured more often. Janzen and Reed (1999) propose that lighter color snails are taken more often by Snail Kites because of their observation of directional selection against lighter color in the snail population. However, this was not the case in this study, indicating that the Kite can locate a dark shell just as easily as it can locate a lighter one. This would imply the presence of more important visual cues than contrast in color on the surface of the habitat. During our study, we observed that snails floating on the surface of the marsh were generally floating operculum side up, which would also support the fact that color of the shell provides no consistent visual cue for the Snail Kite.
